items.title: Joe Mares Jr. Interview, 1960-04-08
items.q: I got the job for Johnny Wiggs and his outfit... I'm going to do a little recording this band.

ctx.x: Where were most of them done, if you don't mind telling? Well, at different spots, Bill. Any trade secrets? No, no, there's no trade, too. I mean, you know what I mean. It would be interesting for people someday to know, because on the label it doesn't tell exactly, and nobody usually tells, and they won't know unless someone like you will tell them.

Well, my 207 and Mardi Gras Parade music from New Orleans, we have things like King Zulu, and I'll Cease to Love and those tunes, and we made that at the Woodman and Royal Hall. It's a big open hall, and naturally we had to get the outside effect, and sort of an echoes outside, and we used the big hall for that. I've done probably eight or ten of them at WDSU here in New Orleans. I've used, lately I've used Dan's Pierce 600 at 501 Boybman Street, where Al Hoyt appears nightly. The acoustics are very, very fine…
At the Legion Hall. I thought maybe it was at Lentz or something. No, no, it was across the street from Lentz.

items.title: Joe Mares Jr. Interview, 1960-04-08
items.q: I have all of them, like Johnny Wig, Sharky, Santo Pacora.

ctx.x: Even Al Hurt never recorded before you did, did he?

That's right. I gave Al Hurt his first break on the Southland label. Pete Fountain fronted his first band on my little label. Jack Delaney, Raymond Boyk. Well, there's a lot of fellas that got their first start with Southland. And they went on to bigger and better things with different recording companies. I have all of them, like Johnny Wig, Sharky, Santo Pacora. And most of the top, not most, but all the top boys around New Orleans. My only regret is that I wasn't able to get Paul, my brother. Paul passed on,…
Mind you, the beginning of your life, the starting, when you were born, where you were raised, what part of town and all? A little bit about your father and your family.
